stem: Identify the growth hormone in plants which causes inhibitory effect.
solution:
**(B)** Abscissic acid

Abscissic acid (ABA) is the natural growth inhibiting hormone of plants. It induces dormancy of buds and seeds by inhibiting growth processes, inhibits and delays cell division and cell elongation, suppresses the activity of the vascular cambium and promotes abscission and senescence. The textbook lists ethylene also as a growth inhibitor along with ABA, but ABA is the hormone described as the natural growth inhibiting hormone, while cytokinins and gibberellins are growth promoters.

stem: Which one of the following is not a part of lac operon?
solution:
**(C)** Inducer

The lac operon of E. coli consists of the regulator gene, the promoter gene, the operator gene and the structural genes. The inducer (allolactose, formed from lactose) is a chemical present in the cytoplasm which inactivates the repressor protein. It switches the operon on but is not a component of the operon.

chapter: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Animals
stem: In absence of fertilization, corpus luteum degenerates into _____.
solution:
**(D)** corpus albicans

After ovulation the ruptured Graafian follicle forms the corpus luteum. If fertilization does not take place, the corpus luteum degenerates into a white scar called corpus albicans.

stem: Which of the following divides nasal cavity?
solution:
**(B)** Mesethmoid cartilage

The nasal cavity is divided into right and left nasal chambers by the mesethmoid cartilage. Each nasal chamber is further divided into vestibule, respiratory part and olfactory part.

stem: Which of the following is caused by unsterilized needle?
solution:
**(B)** AIDS

HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, is transmitted through blood, by blood transfusion, needle sharing or accidental needle injury, so an unsterilized needle can transmit AIDS. Elephantiasis (filariasis), malaria and dengue are transmitted by the bite of mosquitoes.

stem: Recognition sequence of restriction enzymes are generally _____ nucleotides long.
solution:
**(B)** 4 to 8

The sequences recognized by restriction enzymes are 4 to 8 nucleotides long and show a particular type of internal symmetry called a palindrome, e.g. the sequence recognized by EcoRI.

chapter: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Plants
stem: Which of the following types require pollinator but result is genetically similar to autogamy?
solution:
**(A)** Geitonogamy

Geitonogamy is the transfer of pollen grains to the stigma of a different flower produced on the same plant. It is functionally similar to cross pollination because it needs a pollinating agent, but it is genetically similar to autogamy because the pollen grains come from the same plant, so it brings about no genetic variation.

stem: Which one of the following does not evolve further?
solution:
**(A)** Climax community

Ecological succession proceeds through pioneer species and a series of seral communities and finally reaches a stable climax community. The climax community does not evolve further.

stem: Identify the appropriate term for the number of births under ideal conditions :
solution:
**(D)** Absolute natality

Absolute natality is the number of births under ideal conditions, that is, with no competition and with abundant resources such as food and water. The number of births when environmental pressures operate is realized natality.

stem: Observe the graph and select correct option :

options.label: B
options.text: Line ‘B’ represents \(\log C = \log A + Z \log S\)

options.label: D
options.text: Line B represents \(\log S = \log Z + C \log A\)

solution:
**(C)** Line A represents \(S = CA^{Z}\)

In the species-area relationship, species richness \(S\) increases with area \(A\) only up to a certain limit. On ordinary axes this relationship is a rectangular hyperbola, the curve A, given by \(S = CA^{Z}\), where C is the Y-intercept and Z is the slope. On a log-log scale the same relationship becomes the straight line B, given by \(\log S = \log C + Z \log A\).

stem: What are vestigeal organs?
solution: Vestigial organs are imperfectly developed, non-functional, degenerate structures which were functional in related animals or in the ancestors, e.g. nictitating membrane, wisdom teeth (third molars) and coccyx in human beings.

chapter: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Animals
stem: Expand the term ZIFT.
solution: ZIFT: Zygote Intrafallopian Transfer.

stem: Give the name of endocrine gland which is prominent at birth but gets gradually atrophied in adult stage.
solution: Thymus gland. It is prominent at birth but gradually atrophies in the adult, so it is called a temporary gland.

stem: What is the full form of IAA?
solution: IAA: Indole-3-acetic acid, the most common natural auxin.

subtopic: Role of Microbes in Industrial Production
stem: Give the name of microbial source of antibiotic chloromycetin.
solution: The antibiotic chloromycetin is obtained from Streptomyces venezuelae.

stem: Which cells of islets of Langerhans produce a hormone insulin?
solution: Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans (about 70% of the islet cells) secrete insulin.

chapter: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Plants
stem: How many meiotic divisions are required for the formation of 300 seeds in angiosperm?
solution:
Each seed develops from one fertilized ovule, and each ovule needs one functional megaspore (embryo sac) and one pollen grain.

- Female side: one megaspore mother cell undergoes one meiosis to form a tetrad of megaspores, of which only one is functional. For 300 seeds, 300 meiotic divisions are needed.
- Male side: one microspore mother cell undergoes one meiosis to form a tetrad of 4 pollen grains. For 300 pollen grains, \(300 \div 4 = 75\) meiotic divisions are needed.

\(\therefore\) Total meiotic divisions \(= 300 + 75 = 375\).

stem: Explain the term Emigration.
solution: Emigration is the number of individuals of a population who leave the habitat during the time period under consideration. It decreases the population density.

stem: What are the reasons for the success of Mendel?
solution:
Reasons for Mendel's success:

1. His experiments were carefully planned and involved large samples.
2. He carefully recorded the number of plants of each type and expressed his results in terms of ratios.
3. In the pea plant, contrasting characters can be easily recognized.
4. Each of the seven characters he selected was controlled by a single factor, and the factors were located on separate chromosomes.
5. He studied the traits one at a time or in combination of two or three, and processed the data mathematically and statistically.

stem:
Arrange the following steps of DNA fingerprinting in correct sequence :

(a) Gel electrophoresis

(b) Isolation of DNA

(c) Southern blotting

(d) Restriction digestion
solution:
The correct sequence is:

(b) Isolation of DNA \(\rightarrow\) (d) Restriction digestion \(\rightarrow\) (a) Gel electrophoresis \(\rightarrow\) (c) Southern blotting

1. Isolation of DNA: DNA is recovered from a small amount of tissue such as blood, hair roots or skin.
2. Restriction digestion: restriction enzymes cut the DNA into fragments of variable lengths (RFLP).
3. Gel electrophoresis: the fragments are separated on agarose gel according to their length, forming bands.
4. Southern blotting: the separated fragments are transferred to a nylon membrane or nitrocellulose filter paper.

chapter: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Animals
stem: Distinguish between human sperm and ovum.
solution:
| Human sperm | Human ovum |
|---|---|
| Male gamete, formed in the testis by spermatogenesis. | Female gamete, formed in the ovary by oogenesis. |
| Motile, microscopic, elongated cell. | Non-motile, rounded cell, about 0.1 mm (100 microns) in size. |
| Divisible into head, neck, middle piece and tail. | Not divided into parts; has a large nucleus (germinal vesicle) and cytoplasm (ooplasm). |
| Head bears an acrosome containing hydrolytic enzymes. | Acrosome absent. |
| Centrioles present; middle piece has spirally coiled mitochondria. | Devoid of centrioles. |
| No egg membranes. | Surrounded by vitelline membrane, zona pellucida and corona radiata. |

stem: Enlist the uses of gene therapy.
solution:
Gene therapy is the treatment of a disorder by replacing, altering or supplementing a gene that is absent or abnormal. It is used to:

1. Replace missing or defective genes.
2. Deliver genes that speed up the destruction of cancer cells.
3. Supply genes that cause cancer cells to revert back to normal cells.
4. Deliver bacterial or viral genes as a form of vaccination.
5. Supply genes for impairing viral replication.
6. Provide genes that promote or impede the growth of new tissue, and deliver genes that stimulate the healing of damaged tissue.

stem:
Define the following terms :

(a) Gene flow

(b) Chromosomal aberrations
solution:
(a) Gene flow: Gene flow is the movement of genes into or out of a population. It may occur by migration of organisms, dispersal of gametes (pollen) or transfer of segments of DNA, and it alters the gene frequency of the population.

(b) Chromosomal aberrations: The changes in chromosome number (gains and losses) and the changes in the structure of chromosomes constitute chromosomal aberrations. Structural changes are deletion (loss of a segment), duplication (repeat of a segment), inversion (reversal of a segment) and translocation (movement of a segment to another chromosome).

chapter: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Plants
stem: What are the significances of double fertilization?
solution:
Significance of double fertilization:

1. It is a unique feature of angiosperms. It ensures that the parent plant invests a seed with a food store only if the egg is fertilized.
2. The diploid zygote formed by syngamy develops into an embryo, which develops into a new plant.
3. The triploid primary endosperm nucleus formed by triple fusion develops into the nutritive endosperm tissue.
4. It restores the diploid condition by fusion of the haploid male gamete with the haploid egg.
5. It helps to avoid polyembryony.

subtopic: Path of Water Across the Root
stem: Identify and define ‘A’ and ‘B’ in relation to uptake of water by the root :
solution:
A: Symplast pathway. When water passes across the root from one living cell to another living cell through plasmodesmata, it is called the symplast pathway. In the figure, path A begins inside the root hair cell and runs through the cells.

B: Apoplast pathway. When water passes across the root through the cell walls and intercellular spaces of the cortical cells, it is called the apoplast pathway. It is a non-living pathway and occurs only up to the endodermis, where the Casparian strip forces water into the symplast. In the figure, path B runs along the cell walls.

stem: Describe mutualism.
solution:
Mutualism is an interaction between two species in which both species are benefited. It is obligatory and interdependent.

- Lichens show an intimate mutualistic relationship between a fungus and photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria.
- Plants need animals for pollination of flowers and dispersal of seeds, and the animals are rewarded with pollen, nectar and juicy, nutritious fruits.
- Such plant-animal interactions often involve co-evolution, as the evolution of a flower and its pollinator are tightly linked.

stem: Explain factors affecting water absorption.
solution:
Factors affecting water absorption:

1. Presence of capillary water in the soil is essential for absorption.
2. The rate of water absorption is maximum at a soil temperature between \(20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and \(30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).
3. A high concentration of solutes in soil water reduces the rate of absorption of water.
4. Poorly aerated soil shows a poor rate of absorption.
5. Increased transpiration accelerates the rate of absorption of water in irrigated soil.

stem: What is differentiation and redifferentiation?
solution:
Differentiation: The permanent change in the structure and function of cells derived from the apical meristems of root and shoot, leading to maturation, is called differentiation. The cells lose the capacity to divide, e.g. parenchyma in hydrophytes develops large intercellular spaces for buoyancy and aeration.

Redifferentiation: The cells produced by dedifferentiation once again lose the capacity to divide and mature to perform specific functions. This is called redifferentiation, e.g. secondary xylem and secondary phloem formed from the dedifferentiated cambium.

stem:
Select and rewrite appropriate disorder of respiratory system with the given symptoms :

[ sinusitis, emphysema, silicosis and asbestosis, laryngitis ]

(a) Breakdown of alveoli, shortness of breath.

(b) Inflammation of the sinuses, mucous discharge.

(c) Inflammation of larynx, vocal cord, sore throat, hoarseness of voice, mucous build up and cough.

(d) Inflammation of fibrosis, lung damage.
solution:
(a) Breakdown of alveoli, shortness of breath: emphysema.

(b) Inflammation of the sinuses, mucous discharge: sinusitis.

(c) Inflammation of larynx, vocal cord, sore throat, hoarseness of voice, mucous build up and cough: laryngitis.

(d) Inflammation of fibrosis, lung damage: silicosis and asbestosis.

stem: Explain the steps involved in preliminary treatment of sewage.
solution:
The preliminary treatment of sewage includes screening and the grit chamber.

1. Screening: Sewage contains suspended and floating materials and coarse solid particles. The sewage is passed through screens or nets in screening chambers, which hold back the larger suspended and floating objects so that they can be removed before biological treatment.
2. Grit chamber: The screened sewage is then passed through a series of grit chambers containing large stones (pebbles) and brick-ballast. The coarse particles settle down by gravity, removing much of the coarse particulate matter.

stem: Give the different steps involved in formation of m-RNA from hn-RNA.
solution:
In eukaryotes the primary transcript, hnRNA (heterogeneous nuclear RNA), is non-functional and contains both exons (coding sequences) and introns (non-coding sequences). It is processed into m-RNA by the following steps:

1. Splicing: the introns are removed and the exons are joined together in a definite sequence by a ligase enzyme.
2. Capping: methylated guanosine triphosphate is added to the 5' end of hnRNA.
3. Tailing: polyadenylation takes place at the 3' end, adding a poly A tail.

The fully processed hnRNA is now called m-RNA, and it is transported out of the nucleus through the nuclear pore for translation.

stem: What is reproductive isolation? Describe any two types each of pre-mating and post-mating isolating mechanism.
solution:
Reproductive isolation is the isolation that prevents interbreeding between populations. It occurs due to change in the genetic material, gene pool and structure of the genital organs.

A. Pre-mating (pre-zygotic) isolating mechanisms prevent fertilization and zygote formation:

1. Habitat (ecological) isolation: members of a population live in the same geographic region but occupy separate habitats, so potential mates do not meet.
2. Seasonal (temporal) isolation: members live in the same region but become sexually mature in different years or at different times of the year.

B. Post-mating (post-zygotic) isolating mechanisms:

1. Zygote mortality: the egg is fertilized but the zygote dies.
2. Hybrid sterility: the hybrids develop to maturity but are sterile due to failure of proper gametogenesis, e.g. the mule.

stem: Explain unique features of acquired immunity.
solution:
Acquired (adaptive or specific) immunity is the resistance that an individual acquires during life. Its unique features are:

1. Specificity: it produces a specific antibody or T-lymphocyte against a particular antigen or pathogen.
2. Diversity: it can recognize a vast variety of diverse pathogens or foreign molecules.
3. Discrimination between self and non-self: it differentiates between the body's own cells (self) and foreign (non-self) molecules.
4. Memory: on the first encounter with a pathogen, the immune system generates a response and eliminates it, and it retains the memory of this encounter. A second encounter with the same pathogen brings about a quicker and stronger immune response.

stem: Name and describe hormones secreted by ovaries.
solution:
The ovaries secrete the following hormones:

1. Estrogen: secreted by the developing follicle; estradiol is the main estrogen. It is responsible for the secondary sexual characters in the female.
2. Progesterone: secreted by the corpus luteum after ovulation. It thickens the uterine endometrium, preparing the uterus for implantation; it develops the mammary glands during pregnancy and inhibits uterine contractions during pregnancy.
3. Relaxin: secreted by the corpus luteum at the end of gestation. It relaxes the cervix and the ligaments of the pelvic girdle for easy birth.
4. Inhibin: secreted by the corpus luteum. It inhibits the production of FSH and GnRH.

stem: Explain different steps involved in PCR technique.
solution:
PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is the in vitro amplification of a desired DNA segment, carried out in a thermal cycler. The reaction mixture contains the DNA segment to be amplified, the four deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs), an excess of two primers, heat-stable (Taq) DNA polymerase and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ions. The steps are:

1. Denaturation: the mixture is heated to 90 to 98 \(^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), which separates the two strands of the DNA.
2. Annealing: the mixture is cooled to 40 to 60 \(^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), so that the primers pair with the complementary sequences on the single strands.
3. Primer extension: at 70 to 75 \(^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), Taq DNA polymerase uses each single strand as a template and adds nucleotides to the primer.

One cycle takes about 3 to 4 minutes and doubles the DNA. The cycle is repeated automatically 20 to 30 times, so \(n\) cycles produce \(2^{n}\) copies of the DNA segment. The amplified DNA is then purified by gel electrophoresis.

stem: Identify A, B, and C from the above diagrams and give their functions.
solution:
| Cell | Identification | Function |
|---|---|---|
| A | Neutrophil: granulocyte with very fine, evenly distributed granules and a nucleus with several lobes. | Performs amoeboid movement and phagocytosis, destroying pathogens. |
| B | Eosinophil (acidophil): granulocyte with granules and a bilobed nucleus. | Destroys antigen-antibody complexes by phagocytosis, shows antihistaminic property in allergy and produces antitoxins for detoxification. |
| C | Monocyte: largest agranulocyte with a large bean or kidney shaped nucleus and no granules. | Actively motile; gives rise to macrophages and destroys bacteria and dead or damaged tissue by phagocytosis. |

stem: What are the limitations of root pressure theory?
solution:
Limitations (objections) of root pressure theory:

1. It is not applicable to plants taller than 20 metres, since a root pressure of +1 to +2 bars can raise water only 10 to 20 metres.
2. Ascent of sap can occur even in the absence of a root system.
3. Root pressure is almost zero in tall gymnosperm trees.
4. No root pressure is developed in actively transpiring plants.
5. Under normal conditions the xylem sap is under tension, that is, it shows a negative hydrostatic pressure.

Hence root pressure is not the sole mechanism of ascent of sap.

stem: Explain green house effect with reference to gases responsible for it and their sources.
solution:
Greenhouse effect: Part of the solar radiation reaching the earth heats its surface, and the surface re-emits the heat as infrared radiation. Atmospheric gases absorb a major part of this radiation and radiate heat back to the earth's surface, reheating it. Since the atmosphere acts like the glass wall of a greenhouse, this is called the greenhouse effect. Without it the average temperature of the earth would be \(-18^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) instead of \(15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).

Gases responsible and their sources:

1. Carbon dioxide \((\mathrm{CO_2})\): burning of fossil fuels in industries and automobiles, and burning of agricultural wastes.
2. Methane \((\mathrm{CH_4})\): biogas plants, paddy fields and cattle sheds.
3. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs): fire extinguishers and air conditioners.
4. Nitrous oxide \((\mathrm{N_2O})\) and water vapour also contribute.

An increase in these gases heats the earth, causing global warming.

stem: Describe physiological effects and applications of ethylene.
solution:
Ethylene is the only gaseous growth regulator. Its physiological effects and applications are:

1. It promotes ripening of fruits like bananas, apples and mangoes.
2. It stimulates initiation of lateral roots and breaks the dormancy of buds and seeds.
3. It accelerates abscission of leaves, flowers and fruits by forming the abscission layer.
4. It inhibits the growth of lateral buds, causing apical dominance, and enhances senescence of plant organs.
5. It inhibits flowering in most plants except pineapple, and causes epinasty (drooping) of leaves and flowers.
6. It increases the activity of chlorophyllase, causing degreening of banana and Citrus fruits. Ethephon, which releases ethylene in water, is the most widely used source of ethylene.

stem: Give the name and type of I, IV and VII cranial nerves.
solution:
| Number | Name | Type | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | Olfactory | Sensory | Smell (from the epithelium of the nose) |
| IV | Pathetic | Motor | Rotation and movement of the eye ball |
| VII | Facial | Mixed | Facial expression, secretion of tears and saliva, taste |

stem: Describe pyramid of energy with the help of diagram.
solution:
The pyramid of energy shows the amount of energy accumulated per unit area at successive trophic levels of a food chain.

Diagram (described in words): a stepped pyramid of four horizontal bars, widest at the base and narrowest at the apex, labelled from the base upward:

| Trophic level | Energy |
|---|---|
| Tertiary consumers (apex) | 0.1% |
| Secondary consumers | 1% |
| Primary consumers | 10% |
| Producers (base) | 100% |

When energy flows from one trophic level to the next, only about 10% passes on as net energy, and a large amount is lost as heat at each step. Hence the pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted. Shorter food chains therefore have more energy available than longer ones.

stem: What is lac? Enlist economic importance of Lac.
solution:
Lac is a resin-like substance secreted by the dermal glands of the female lac insect, *Tachardia lacca*. The insect feeds on succulent twigs of plants like ber, peepal, palas, kusum and babool and secretes a pink resin which hardens on contact with air to form lac. It contains a large amount of resin with sugar, water, minerals and alkaline substances. Shellac is the pure form of lac obtained by washing and filtering.

Economic importance of lac:

1. Lac is used in making bangles and toys.
2. It is used in woodwork, inks and mirrors.
3. The lac insect is native to India, and India produces about 85% of the world's lac.
4. Lac products play a vital role in the economy of farmers.

chapter: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Animals
stem: Describe histological structure of Testis with well labelled diagram.
solution:
Histology of testis:

1. Coverings: The testis is covered externally by a collagenous connective tissue layer, the tunica albuginea. Outer to it is an incomplete peritoneal covering, the tunica vaginalis, and inner to it is the thin, vascular tunica vasculosa.
2. Lobules: Fibres from the tunica albuginea divide each testis into about 200 to 300 testicular lobules, each containing 1 to 4 highly coiled seminiferous tubules.
3. Seminiferous tubules: Each tubule is lined internally by cuboidal germinal epithelial cells (spermatogonia) resting on a basement membrane, and a few large pyramidal Sertoli (sustentacular) cells. The germinal cells undergo spermatogenesis, so spermatogonia, primary spermatocytes, secondary spermatocytes, spermatids and sperms are seen from the periphery towards the lumen. Sertoli cells provide nutrition to the developing sperms.
4. Interstitial cells: Leydig cells lie in the connective tissue between the seminiferous tubules and secrete the male hormone testosterone.

Diagram (T.S. of testis, described in words): draw a few circular seminiferous tubules in section surrounded by connective tissue, with the tunica albuginea as the outer covering. Labels to show: tunica albuginea, connective tissue, seminiferous tubule, basement membrane, germinal epithelium, Sertoli cell, sperm bundle in the lumen, interstitial (Leydig) cells.

stem: What are chromosomal disorders? Describe Turner’s syndrome and Klinefelter’s syndrome.
solution:
Chromosomal disorders are disorders caused by the absence or excess of one or more chromosomes or by their abnormal arrangement, e.g. Down's syndrome, Turner's syndrome and Klinefelter's syndrome.

Turner's syndrome (44 + XO):

- It is a sex chromosomal disorder (X monosomy) caused by non-disjunction of chromosomes during formation of the egg.
- The individual has 44 autosomes with XO and is phenotypically female.
- Features: short stature, webbed neck, low posterior hair line, broad shield-shaped chest, poorly developed ovaries and breasts, and low intelligence.

Klinefelter's syndrome (44 + XXY):

- It is caused by an extra X chromosome in males, resulting from non-disjunction of the X chromosome during meiosis in the formation of the ovum.
- The individual is male with overall masculine development but is described as a feminized male.
- Features: tall stature with long arms, underdeveloped testes, development of breasts (gynaecomastia) and no spermatogenesis, so the individual is sterile.

stem: Describe nervous system in planaria with well labelled diagram.
solution:
Planaria is a flatworm of phylum Platyhelminthes and is the most primitive animal with a central nervous system, which lies on the ventral side of the body.

1. Brain: a mass of cerebral (cephalic) ganglia in the head region forms an inverted U-shaped brain. Nine branches arise from each ganglion towards the outer side.
2. Ventral nerve cords: a pair of long ventral nerve cords arises from below the ganglia and runs along the body.
3. Transverse nerves: the nerve cords are interconnected by transverse nerves (commissures) in a ladder-like manner, so it is called a ladder type nervous system.
4. Peripheral nervous system: a peripheral nerve plexus arises laterally from the nerve cords, and sensory cells are arranged in lateral cords and scattered in the body.
5. Eyes: a pair of photosensory eyes (eyespots) lies on the dorsal side of the brain.

Diagram (described in words): draw the outline of the flatworm with the inverted U-shaped brain in the head region, two nerve cords running back along the body joined by cross connections like the rungs of a ladder, and two eyespots over the brain. Labels to show: eyespot, brain, nerve cords, transverse nerve.

chapter: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Plants
stem:
Explain following terms :

(a) Grafting

(b) Apomixis

(c) Polyembryony

(d) Parthenocarpy
solution:
(a) Grafting: Grafting is a method of vegetative propagation in which parts of two plants are joined so that they grow as one plant. A part of the stem with more than one bud (scion) is joined onto a rooted plant (stock), e.g. apple, pear, rose.

(b) Apomixis: Apomixis is the formation of embryo(s) through an asexual method of reproduction without formation of gametes and without fertilization, that is, without meiosis and syngamy. The embryo develops in the ovule and the ovule forms the seed. Genetically identical plants can be produced rapidly by apomixis.

(c) Polyembryony: Polyembryony is the development of more than one embryo inside a seed, which results in the emergence of multiple seedlings, e.g. Citrus. The extra embryos may arise from cells of the nucellus or integuments (adventive polyembryony) or by cleavage of the zygote proembryo (cleavage polyembryony). It increases the chances of survival of new plants.

(d) Parthenocarpy: Parthenocarpy is the development of fruit without fertilization, so the fruit is seedless. It occurs naturally in some varieties of pineapple, banana and papaya, where the placental tissue produces auxin (IAA) which enlarges the ovary into a fruit. It can be induced artificially by spraying gibberellins, delaying pollination or using foreign pollen.

stem: Interpret the given diagrams A and B. Enlist the changes occuring during inspiration and expiration.
solution:
Diagram A shows inspiration: air enters the lungs through the trachea and the diaphragm moves downward (arrow pointing down). Diagram B shows expiration: air leaves the lungs and the diaphragm moves upward (arrow pointing up).

| Inspiration (A) | Expiration (B) |
|---|---|
| Atmospheric air is taken into the lungs. | Air from the lungs is exhaled. |
| Diaphragm contracts, becomes flat and moves downward. | Diaphragm relaxes, becomes dome shaped and is pushed upward. |
| External intercostal muscles contract. | Intercostal muscles relax. |
| Ribs and sternum move upward and outward. | Rib cage moves inward and downward. |
| Thoracic volume increases. | Thoracic volume decreases. |
| Pressure in the thorax and lungs decreases below atmospheric pressure, so air rushes in. | Pressure in the thorax and lungs increases above atmospheric pressure, so air rushes out. |
| It is an active process. | The muscles relax during normal expiration. |
